content: By the age of one month, medically stable preterm infants, regardless of their initial birth weight or gestational age, exhibit a vaccination response comparable to that of full-term infants. In pediatric hemodialysis patients, data on their response to standard pediatric vaccine doses are limited. However, protective antibody levels are achieved in 75% to 97% of patients who receive higher doses (20 µg) of the vaccine, either on a three-dose or four-dose schedule. For immunocompromised individuals, such as hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, patients undergoing chemotherapy, and HIV-infected persons, modified dosing regimens—such as doubling the standard antigen dose or administering additional doses—may improve response rates. However, data on the efficacy of these alternative vaccination schedules remain limited. Anti-HBs is the only easily measurable correlate of vaccine-induced protection. Immunocompetent individuals who achieve anti-HBs concentrations greater than 10 mIU/mL after preexposure vaccination are nearly completely protected against both acute disease and chronic infection, even if their anti-HBs concentrations later decline to below 10 mIU/mL. Although immunogenicity is lower among immunocompromised individuals, those who achieve and maintain a protective antibody response before exposure to HBV are highly protected from infection. After primary immunization with the hepatitis B vaccine, anti-HBs concentrations decline rapidly within the first year and more slowly thereafter. Among children who respond to a primary vaccine series with antibody levels greater than 10 mIU/mL, 15% to 50% experience low or undetectable anti-HBs concentrations (anti-HBs loss) 5 to 15 years after vaccination. The persistence of detectable anti-HBs after vaccination, in the absence of HBV exposure, depends on the level of post-vaccination antibody concentration. Despite declines in anti-HBs to below 10 mIU/mL, nearly all vaccinated individuals remain protected against HBV infection. The mechanism for continued vaccine-induced protection is thought to involve the preservation of immune memory through the selective expansion and differentiation of antigen-specific B and T lymphocyte clones. The persistence of vaccine-induced immune memory has been demonstrated among individuals who responded to a primary childhood vaccine series 13 to 23 years earlier but later had anti-HBs levels below 10 mIU/mL. This was evidenced by an anamnestic increase in anti-HBs levels in 67% to 76% of these individuals 2 to 4 weeks after receiving an additional vaccine dose. Although direct measurement of immune memory is not yet possible, these data suggest that a high proportion of vaccine recipients retain immune memory and would develop an anti-HBs response upon exposure to HBV. Studies of immunocompetent individuals vaccinated as children or infants indicate that, despite anti-HBs loss years after immunization, nearly all vaccinated individuals who respond to a primary series remain protected from HBV infection. No clinical cases of hepatitis B have been observed in follow-up studies conducted 15 to 20 years after vaccination among immunocompetent individuals with antibody levels greater than 10 mIU/mL. Certain studies have documented breakthrough infections (detected by the presence of anti-HBc or HBV DNA) in a small percentage of vaccinated individuals. However, these infections are usually transient and asymptomatic, with chronic infections documented only rarely. Breakthrough infections resulting in chronic infection have been observed only among vaccinated infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers. No clinically significant HBV infections have been documented among immunocompromised individuals who maintain protective levels of anti-HBs. In studies of long-term protection among HIV-infected individuals, breakthrough infections have occurred after a decline in anti-HBs concentrations to below 10 mIU/mL. Both passive-active postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) with hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and hepatitis B vaccine, and active PEP with the hepatitis B vaccine alone, have been shown to be highly effective in preventing transmission after exposure to HBV. HBIG alone has also been demonstrated to be effective in preventing HBV transmission, but with the availability of the hepatitis B vaccine, HBIG is typically used as an adjunct to vaccination. The major determinant of PEP effectiveness is the early administration of the initial vaccine dose. The effectiveness of PEP diminishes the longer it is initiated after exposure. Studies on the maximum interval after exposure during which PEP remains effective are limited, but the interval is unlikely to exceed 7 days for perinatal and needlestick exposures and 14 days for sexual exposures.
